pre_mortem.summary: The plan rests almost entirely on untested behavioral and market assumptions: that students at a single UK campus will both list and rent study items from peers, that a 10% fee is acceptable, and that customers can be acquired without a defined channel. The most likely failure is a liquidity collapse at launch—insufficient listings or renters at the pilot university leading to zero transactions. Before building, the founder must validate demand, willingness to pay, and repeatable acquisition on the ground with cheap, early experiments.

flaws.title: Critical: Marketplace liquidity will not materialize at a single campus
flaws.description: The strategy assumes a two-sided marketplace can reach the required density from day one at one university, but there is no evidence of supply (students willing to list items) or demand (students willing to rent from peers). The killing-blow scenario is launch with few or no listings and few renters, producing no transactions and collapsing any network effects. At idea stage this is fatal because a marketplace cannot function without a plan or evidence for both sides before build.
flaws.question: What exact minimum numbers of listings and active renters are required to make the pilot viable, and how will you prove you can recruit both sides before building the product?

flaws.title: High: No evidence students actually want peer-to-peer rentals
flaws.description: Founder relies solely on personal experience and has not interviewed or surveyed target students, so demand is assumed rather than demonstrated. Students' revealed preferences may be to buy used, borrow for free, rely on university services, or use digital resources — any of which would undercut the rental model. Without even basic qualitative evidence, the core value proposition is unproven.
flaws.question: Do representative students at the pilot campus prefer renting study items from peers over their current behaviors, and why would they switch?

flaws.title: High: Acquisition channels are undefined; assumption of organic campus growth
flaws.description: The plan leaves unanswered how the first customers will find the marketplace, implicitly assuming campus virality or word-of-mouth will supply both sides. If organic adoption doesn't appear immediately, there is no fallback and the pilot will not reach necessary density. This dependency on an unspecified, fragile acquisition channel is a likely cause of failure.
flaws.question: Specifically how will you acquire the first listings and renters at the pilot university (channels, expected conversion rates, and cost to test) before building the platform?

flaws.title: High: Pricing model (10% fee) and who pays it are untested
flaws.description: A 10% fee is stated without evidence that owners or renters will accept it, or which side will bear the cost. Willingness to pay for peer-to-peer rental services may be low or asymmetric (owners vs renters), and incorrect assumptions here would break revenue and value dynamics. This untested pricing assumption could deter listings or rentals once the product is live.
flaws.question: Who will pay the 10% fee (owner, renter, split), and what evidence shows that target users accept that fee at the pilot campus?

flaws.title: Medium: Current alternatives and revealed preferences are unknown
flaws.description: The founder hasn't identified what students currently do to obtain textbooks, calculators and equipment (buy new/used, borrow, use library/university services, or digital materials). Without mapping existing solutions and why they succeed, the offering may not address the real unmet need or could be a poor fit for behaviors that are hard to change. Misreading stated preference (would you rent?) vs revealed preference (what you actually do) is a likely misstep.
flaws.question: What do students currently use today to obtain these items, and what behaviors must change for them to adopt peer rentals?

flaws.title: Medium: Unclear who the primary customer is (owner vs renter) and how value is delivered
flaws.description: The document doesn't specify whether the product is designed to primarily solve a problem for owners (monetizing unused textbooks) or renters (cheaper access), nor how trust, pickup, and damage-risk will be handled. If the core value proposition isn't targeted to a real pain point for a clear buyer, onboarding and retention will suffer. This ambiguity obscures which tests to run and which metrics matter.
flaws.question: Which side of the marketplace is the primary customer (owner or renter), what exact problem are you solving for them, and how will you validate that solution cheaply?

evidence_audit.summary: Evidence base: Weak. The founder provides only personal experience and no measured demand, pricing, acquisition, or numeric targets for the launch university. The single most important gap is lack of any measured demand or conversion data at the target university, which prevents credible revenue or growth projections. Several load‑bearing inputs (who pays, average price, CAC, behavioral assumptions) are also missing.

flaws.title: No validated demand at the launch university
flaws.description: The founder reports zero interviews or surveys and offers only personal experience as evidence. For a marketplace, even an idea-stage plan must show measurable student interest at the chosen university before building. Without counts (e.g., signups, survey responses or commitments) the central hypothesis—that students will supply and rent items peer‑to‑peer—is unsupported.
flaws.question: Provide measured demand evidence from the target university: how many students were surveyed/interviewed, what percent said they would use a student-to-student rental marketplace, and how many signups/commitments (email/holds/pre‑rents) do you currently have?

flaws.title: Who pays and how much per transaction is unspecified
flaws.description: The document states a 10% fee but does not say whether renters or lenders pay it, nor the expected average rental price. Revenue per transaction = 10% × average price. Even using a conservative labeled assumption (example: average rental price P = £10), revenue = £1 per transaction; to earn £1,000/month you'd need 1,000 transactions. Without the actual payer and average price the fee alone is meaningless.
flaws.question: State who pays the 10% fee (renter or lender) and provide an evidence‑based estimate of the average rental price per transaction at your launch university (or measured willingness‑to‑pay data)?

flaws.title: No acquisition plan, CAC or early conversion targets
flaws.description: The founder skipped how first customers will find the platform. You cannot assess viability without a channel, expected conversion rates, or a CAC bound. For example, to reach 500 transacting users you need defined outreach and conversion (e.g., signups → listings → transactions). With no numbers, required marketing effort and viability are unknown.
flaws.question: Provide a concrete acquisition plan for the first university with expected conversion funnel numbers (impressions → signups → listed items → first transaction) and an estimated CAC per transacting user based on an explicit channel or pilot.

flaws.title: No baseline numeric targets or revenue model provided
flaws.description: The plan lacks load‑bearing key numbers: target transactions per month, first‑year revenue, average item price, and item availability. Revenue formula is Transactions × Avg Price × 10% (take rate). For example, with Avg Price = £15, each transaction yields £1.50; to reach £5,000/term you'd need ≈3,333 transactions. Without targets you can't judge whether the 10% fee and single‑university launch can reach sustainable scale.
flaws.question: Publish baseline numeric targets for the first 12 months: target transactions per month, average rental price, expected listings available, and resulting monthly revenue (using Revenue = transactions × avg price × 10%).

flaws.title: Unclear who the buyer is and which side of the two‑sided market to prioritize
flaws.description: The document does not state whether the primary customer is the renter or the lender (owner). That matters for pricing, acquisition prioritization and trust mechanisms. Two‑sided marketplaces must select which side to subsidize early; this plan gives no evidence or decision on that choice.
flaws.question: Identify the primary paying customer (renter or lender) you will prioritize at launch and provide the rationale or evidence for that choice (e.g., survey data showing willingness to pay or evidence of supply willingness to list).

flaws.title: Key behavioral assumptions are unstated and untested
flaws.description: The plan implicitly assumes students prefer peer rentals over existing options, trust peers to lend/buy back items, and will transact frequently enough. These are load‑bearing behavioral assumptions but are neither named nor tested. At idea stage these should be the first experiments.
flaws.question: List the top 3 behavioral assumptions (e.g., preference for peer rental, trust in peer listings, frequency of rentals) and describe a single low‑cost experiment you will run to validate each one within 4 weeks.

adversarial_competitor.summary: This AI assistant is an obvious bolt-on to existing clinic booking/EHR products and can be neutralized cheaply by incumbents. The plan lacks a defensible differentiator, clear go-to-market detail, and justification for a £149/month charge — all things a well-funded competitor can weaponize quickly. The cheapest kill: ship a simple auto-responder/triage feature bundled into an existing product or offered free to existing customers while leaning on trust and integration partnerships.

flaws.title: Incumbent feature parity makes you redundant
flaws.description: The product is a classic 'feature' (auto-respond/triage for appointment requests) that can be built into any booking/EHR system. A vendor with existing clinic customers can ship a basic AI responder or templates within weeks and mark it as an included capability, removing your primary differentiation. With no claimed unique IP or exclusive data, there's nothing preventing incumbents from replicating core functionality.
flaws.question: What unique capability or data do you have that booking/EHR vendors cannot replicate and ship within 3 months?

flaws.title: We can out-distribute you via existing partnerships and integrations
flaws.description: You plan to integrate with booking systems, but incumbents already own those relationships and integration contracts. A competitor can push the assistant as an add-on or built-in feature across thousands of clinics overnight via existing channels, crushing your GTM. Your document doesn't say which systems or partners you have access to, so you are vulnerable to rapid incumbent rollouts.
flaws.question: Which booking systems are you targeting first and do you have partnership or API access commitments from them?

flaws.title: Price is easily undercut or bundled away
flaws.description: At £149/clinic/month you are attackable: incumbents can include an equivalent feature for free or at a nominal add-on cost, or a deep-pocketed competitor can underprice with freemium to win share. Because clinics are price-sensitive and incumbents can cross-subsidize, your standalone subscription is unlikely to withstand competitive pricing pressure.
flaws.question: Why will clinics pay £149/mo for this instead of getting the same capability bundled by their current vendor or a cheaper alternative?

flaws.title: Brand, trust and patient data concerns favor incumbents
flaws.description: Clinics handle protected health information and will prefer vendors with established compliance, accreditations, and clinical references. A new startup asking to handle patient queries faces a steep trust hurdle; incumbents and NHS-endorsed partners can exploit that to block third-party entrants. Your plan doesn't address compliance, certifications, or clinical endorsements.
flaws.question: How will you overcome clinics' trust and compliance concerns to get them to hand patient queries to a new vendor?

flaws.title: No evidence clinics will pay or adopt — pilot plan missing
flaws.description: There is no demand evidence, pilot commitments, or early adopter pipeline presented. Before launch this should be validated with pay-or-pilot clinics; without that the product is a speculative feature. The cheapest test (not described) would be a concierge pilot with a small number of clinics to prove value and willingness to pay.
flaws.question: How many clinics have agreed to a paid pilot and what metrics will you use to prove value quickly?

flaws.title: Unclear what clinics currently use and how you'll displace them
flaws.description: You haven't specified the incumbent workflows (reception staff, phone systems, automated booking, outsourced triage) you are displacing or augmenting. Without mapping current alternatives, you can't target messaging or product hooks that overcome inertia. That leaves you open to incumbents who already own those workflows.
flaws.question: What are the current workflows and stop-gap solutions clinics use today for appointment requests and patient queries, and which segment will you displace first?

execution_risk.summary: The plan glosses over the hardest parts of shipping: handling regulated patient data, integrating with many heterogeneous booking systems, and actually finding paying clinics. Missing detail on team capability, sequencing (validate demand before heavy engineering), and go-to-market execution are the most likely causes of multi-month delays or a product that never reaches customers.

flaws.title: No plan for regulated patient data (GDPR/medical liability)
flaws.description: The doc says the assistant will handle patient queries and appointment requests but says nothing about legal or compliance work. Processing identifiable health-related data in the UK triggers GDPR, Data Protection Impact Assessments, data processing agreements with clinics, potential registration with ICO, and clinical/legal liability for automated responses — any of which can block deployment or require a full redesign. This is a fatal operational blocker if not resolved before piloting with real clinics.
flaws.question: What specific legal/compliance steps, DPIAs, DPAs, clinical oversight and insurance are in place to process health data and serve patient-facing AI responses in UK clinics?

flaws.title: Integration hell: supporting many booking systems is under-scoped
flaws.description: You plan to integrate with 'existing booking systems' but provide no list, prioritization, or fallback plan. Each vendor may have different APIs, authentication, webhook behaviors, rate limits, or no API at all — building and maintaining connectors is often months of work per system and a continuous maintenance burden. Underestimating this will push launch timelines and consume engineering resources.
flaws.question: Which booking systems will you support in month 1–6 and what is the concrete engineering plan (including fallback/manual flows) for systems without stable APIs?

flaws.title: No team, roles, or capacity stated versus the scope of work
flaws.description: The document names a product and price but no founders, engineers, or compliance/legal resources. Building secure, integrated, and compliant healthcare automation typically requires multiple engineers, a security/DevOps person, and legal/compliance or clinical input; without that stated, the plan is likely under-resourced and will slip. The implicit failure mode is a one- or two-person team trying to do months of specialized work and burning out or shipping unsafe tech.
flaws.question: Who is on the team today (roles and relevant experience) and how many engineer-months are budgeted for integrations, security, and compliance work?

flaws.title: No go-to-market or clinic acquisition plan
flaws.description: You’ve set a price (£149/mo) but have not described how you will reach or convince clinics to sign up. Small private clinics are time-poor and risk-averse; without a channel (B2B sales, partnerships with booking vendors, reseller, or targeted outreach) you can ship a working product and have zero customers. The specific failure mode is product completion followed by months of zero traction because acquisition wasn't built in parallel.
flaws.question: What are the initial acquisition channels and sales process to acquire the first 10–50 UK clinics, and who will run that outreach?

flaws.title: Pricing is unsupported and may not match clinic willingness to pay
flaws.description: Charging £149/month is stated with no evidence of willingness to pay, cost savings to clinics, or comparable benchmarks. If clinics view this as too expensive relative to their margin or existing staff time, conversion will be low. The plausible failure is a technically working product with churn or zero new signups because the price point is wrong.
flaws.question: What evidence or tests support £149/mo as an acceptable price for target clinics (pilot commitments, surveys, or competitor pricing)?

flaws.title: Sequencing: building AI and integrations before validating demand
flaws.description: The strategy assumes clinics want an automated assistant and will pay upfront; there’s no plan to validate demand with a concierge or manual prototype. If clinics prefer a human triage or a simpler integration, you’ll waste months developing complex automation. Failure mode: wasted engineering on features customers don't need.
flaws.question: What is the cheapest way you will validate clinic demand and willingness to pay before building production integrations (e.g., manual handling, landing page, paid pilots)?

flaws.title: Unspecified data model and security controls for patient data
flaws.description: There is no mention of what patient data is stored, how long it is retained, whether conversations are logged, or how keys/encryption are managed. This omission risks later rework if regulators or customers demand stricter controls, or a security incident forces a pause. The concrete failure is having to redesign storage/architecture mid-development, delaying launch.
flaws.question: What data will you store, where will it reside, and what technical controls (encryption, access controls, audit logs) will you implement from day one?

evidence_audit.summary: Evidence base: Weak. The plan is pre-launch with no pilots, customers, or revenue; core claims (demand, pricing, integrations) are asserted but untested. The most important remaining issue is missing measured demand and pricing validation that underpin revenue forecasts.

flaws.title: No evidence clinics want this (demand)
flaws.description: The document asserts the AI will 'help small private clinics manage appointment requests and patient queries' but provides no measured evidence (pilot, interviews, survey, or signed LOI) that clinics face this problem at scale or will adopt an AI assistant. For an idea-stage product this is load-bearing: without basic demand validation the pricing and go-to-market plans are meaningless. Simple discovery (n = 20–50 clinics) or a paid pilot would be the minimal test.
flaws.question: Provide concrete demand evidence: how many UK small private clinics have you interviewed or piloted with, and what fraction expressed willingness to pay or trial the service?

flaws.title: Pricing (£149/mo) is unsourced and unvalidated
flaws.description: The stated price of £149/clinic/month is presented with no supporting data on willingness-to-pay, price sensitivity, or competitor pricing. That price implies £149 × 12 = £1,788 revenue per clinic per year; whether that yields viable unit economics depends entirely on CAC, churn and marginal costs which are unstated. Charging a price with no validation is a load-bearing assumption for revenue forecasts.
flaws.question: Show pricing validation: results of willingness-to-pay tests, competitive price points, or at least pilot conversion at £149/mo (or explain how you chose £149)?

flaws.title: Customer definition ('small private clinics') is too vague
flaws.description: Targeting 'small private clinics in the UK' lacks segmentation (size, specialty, booking volume, tech stack) needed to size the market and design acquisition. Different clinic types will have different needs and budgets; without a clear buyer persona you cannot estimate addressable market, onboarding complexity, or product fit.
flaws.question: Define the target clinic persona(s): clinic size in practitioners, specialties, monthly appointment volume, and current booking systems used for your initial go-to-market cohort.

flaws.title: No customer acquisition plan or CAC assumptions
flaws.description: The doc says 'begin with clinics in the UK' but gives no acquisition channel, conversion rates, or CAC. That prevents any revenue or unit-economics projections. Even a conservative bound — e.g. one outbound rep at £5k/month fully loaded acquiring X clinics — would allow checking feasibility, but no such numbers are provided.
flaws.question: How will you acquire clinics initially and what are your assumed conversion rate and CAC (provide channel-level estimates or pilot conversion data)?

flaws.title: Integration with 'existing booking systems' is asserted but unproven
flaws.description: The plan to integrate with existing booking systems is central but unspecified: which systems, whether they have public APIs, data access, multi-tenant embedding, or commercial terms. Integration complexity and variability across clinic systems could materially affect time-to-launch and deliverability, yet no feasibility or technical constraints are provided.
flaws.question: List the booking systems you plan to integrate with first and provide evidence (API docs, pilot integrations, or partner agreements) that these integrations are technically and contractually feasible within your timeline.

unit_economics.summary: The document states a price (£149/month per clinic) and target (UK small private clinics) but contains no unit-costs, CAC, conversion or evidence of willingness-to-pay. That makes it impossible to evaluate gross margin, payback, or whether the stated price is realistic relative to customer acquisition costs and hidden operational/regulatory expenses. Before launch the team must provide a minimal unit-economics model and simple validation experiments for price and acquisition.

flaws.title: No fully-burdened cost-to-serve per clinic
flaws.description: The plan lists a price but provides no breakdown of the monthly cost to serve one clinic (compute, storage, backups, monitoring, third‑party APIs, SMS/voice, payment fees, customer support time, onboarding). Without these numbers you cannot calculate gross margin or know whether £149/mo covers ongoing costs at any scale. This is a foundational missing input for unit economics.
flaws.question: What is your fully-burdened monthly cost to serve one clinic (itemized: compute, storage, third‑party API usage, payment fees, and per‑clinic support/onboarding costs)?

flaws.title: Pricing is unsupported by evidence of willingness-to-pay
flaws.description: The document fixes a price of £149/mo but provides no evidence (pilot signups, contracts, survey or A/B price tests) that clinics will actually pay that amount. Stating a price without validation risks a mismatch between assumed ARPU and real revenue. Willingness-to-pay is a core revenue assumption that needs at least a few validated commitments before scaling.
flaws.question: How did you validate the £149/month price — do you have pilot commitments, paid trials, signed LOIs, or price‑sensitivity test results from target clinics?

flaws.title: Customer acquisition channels and CAC are unspecified
flaws.description: There is no acquisition plan or channel mix described, so expected CAC is unknown. At a £149/mo price point different channels (self‑serve, inbound content, outbound sales, partnerships) imply very different CAC and sales cycles; without channel assumptions you cannot estimate payback or scalability. The feasibility of the model depends heavily on realistic CAC relative to LTV.
flaws.question: Which specific acquisition channels will you use, what is your expected CAC per clinic on each, and what experiments will you run to validate those CAC assumptions?

flaws.title: Gross margin and payback period not modeled
flaws.description: No unit-economics model is presented (gross margin per clinic, churn, LTV, months to payback). Without combining cost-to-serve, CAC and churn you cannot say whether the business reaches positive gross margins at scale or how long customer acquisition investment takes to recover. This prevents any sensible planning for hiring, marketing spend, or fundraising.
flaws.question: Provide a simple model showing gross margin per clinic, expected monthly churn, LTV, CAC, and months to payback under your base and pessimistic scenarios.

flaws.title: Operational and regulatory costs (moderation, compliance, refunds) are unaccounted
flaws.description: Healthcare/clinic-facing products commonly incur additional costs: data‑protection/GDPR compliance, secure data handling, legal review, clinical content moderation, incident response, refunds/chargebacks and fraud prevention. None of these are mentioned, yet they can materially increase per‑clinic costs and compliance overhead as you scale.
flaws.question: How will you budget for healthcare data compliance, content moderation/clinical oversight, refunds/chargebacks and fraud prevention, and what monthly cost per clinic do you assume for these functions?

pre_mortem.summary: The plan relied on several untested, interlocking assumptions: that technical integrations with clinics' booking systems would be straightforward, that UK private clinics would accept an AI handling patient queries, and that they would pay £149/month. The single most likely killing blow was a failure to achieve reliable, authorized integrations with the booking systems clinics actually use. Other dependencies—regulatory acceptance, a clear buyer within clinics, and an acquisition channel—also did not materialize because they lacked early validation.

flaws.title: Integration dependency collapsed — booking systems weren't open or consistent
flaws.description: The strategy assumed you could integrate with 'existing booking systems' as a matter of engineering work. In the market outcome, the major systems used by target clinics either had no public APIs, required commercial partnerships, or had highly bespoke data models, making reliable two-way sync infeasible within the planned timeline and budget. Without those integrations the assistant couldn't own appointment state or reliably confirm/modify bookings, which is central to the product's value proposition and effectively killed adoption. The immediate test you missed was proving at least one real, authorized integration with representative systems before assuming broad technical feasibility.
flaws.question: Can you demonstrate working, authorized integrations with the specific booking systems used by representative UK private clinics (not just theoretical APIs)?

flaws.title: Demand unvalidated — clinics didn't want AI to handle patient queries
flaws.description: You assumed clinics actively want an AI to manage appointment requests and patient queries, but you never validated whether clinics view that as acceptable for patient-facing communication. In reality many clinics prioritized human touch, feared patient dissatisfaction, or had low volumes that didn't justify automation. The cheapest validation should have been a small paid pilot or simulated concierge test to measure willingness to hand queries to an automated assistant.

flaws.title: Pricing assumption failed — £149/month didn't match willingness to pay

Not identifying the buyer means the product, pricing and go-to-market are all built on different, incompatible assumptions.
flaws.question: Who is the actual paying customer (self-paying beginners, parents, bootcamps, schools, etc.) and how does that buyer's willingness to pay and procurement behavior look?

flaws.title: No plan for acquisition — dependency on unspecified channels
flaws.description: The document lists 'how will your first customers find you' as unknown. The idea implicitly depends on acquiring beginners cheaply enough to validate paid conversion, but acquisition channels (communities, bootcamps, organic search) are untested. If the assumed channels don't reach paying beginners, adoption stalls regardless of product fit.
flaws.question: Which specific channels will reliably reach and convert early beginner users into paid customers, and can those channels be tested cheaply?

flaws.title: Misread market signal: underestimating free alternatives and behavior
flaws.description: There's no evidence the founder assessed how beginners currently solve errors (free LLMs, StackOverflow, instructors, classmates). If beginners habitually use free tools that provide sufficient answers, they may resist paying for a similar explanation-focused product. The idea risks confusing a nice-to-have (simpler explanations) with a must-have.
flaws.question: What do beginners currently do when they hit errors, and why would they switch from those free behaviors to a paid service?

evidence_audit.summary: Evidence base: Weak. The founder has only a concept grounded in personal experience; there is no measured traction, no buyer definition, and no pricing or acquisition evidence. The most important remaining issue is the absence of any measured willingness-to-pay or clear paying-customer evidence to support the $12/month claim.

flaws.title: No measured demand or willingness-to-pay from beginners
flaws.description: The founder states the product is based on personal experience but reports zero interviews, surveys, landing-page tests or paid preorders with beginner programmers. Without measured purchase intent the claim that people will pay $12/month is unsupported. Cheap, decisive tests exist (interviews, landing page with preorders) and none have been reported.
flaws.question: Can you show measured willingness-to-pay from beginner programmers — either detailed notes from at least 20 customer interviews explicitly addressing price, or a live landing page that produced paid preorders (minimum 5 at $12/month) — and share the raw results?

flaws.title: Unspecified paying customer (who actually buys it?)
flaws.description: The document does not define who will pay: self-learners, students, parents, bootcamps or employers. Different buyers have very different willingness-to-pay and buying processes; not naming a buyer leaves the pricing, distribution and messaging unsupported. This is load-bearing because it determines acquisition and revenue assumptions.
flaws.question: Who is the paying customer (a clear buyer persona) for the $12/month product, and what evidence (interviews, purchase intent, or commitments) do you have that that persona will be the purchaser?

flaws.title: Price ($12/mo) given with no supporting basis
flaws.description: You state a $12/month price but provide no evidence or rationale for it. That implies $144/year ARPU per paying user, but LTV, churn and elasticity are unknown; a wrong price would break revenue forecasts or acquisition economics. Pricing decisions must be experimentally validated for an idea-stage product.
flaws.question: What evidence justifies the $12/month price — please provide the raw data from any pricing tests, competitor pricing analysis, or willingness-to-pay interviews that led you to select $12/month?

flaws.title: No plan or evidence for how first customers will be acquired
flaws.description: The founder left acquisition unspecified. For an idea-stage product, the most important early evidence is a repeatable channel that finds the target beginners at acceptable cost. Without even a small acquisition experiment, the funnel and CAC are unknown and the business model is ungrounded.
flaws.question: Show the results of an acquisition experiment (e.g., a landing page, community post, or paid test) that produced at least 10 sign-ups or measurable interest from your target beginners, including the channel, conversions and cost per signup.

flaws.title: No evidence that 'simpler explanations' beat existing tools
flaws.description: The product's differentiation claim (simpler explanations will make you choose it over existing AI coding tools) is asserted but not tested. Without comparative user tests or qualitative evidence, it's unknown whether simpler explanations actually improve comprehension or are preferred by beginners in practice.
flaws.question: Provide results from a comparative user test showing your explanations outperform a leading alternative on beginner comprehension or task success (for example, measured completion time, correctness, or self-reported understanding across ~20 users).

unit_economics.summary: The provided numbers (£5/month price, £2 compute per generated video, 20 videos/user/month) imply dramatically negative unit economics: compute cost alone is £40/user/month versus £5 revenue. The plan omits essential per-user costs (storage, CDN, support, payments), any evidence customers will pay £5 for unlimited generation, and any CAC/activation assumptions — all of which must be specified and tested before this is viable.

flaws.title: Price vs stated compute cost yields immediate, large negative margin
flaws.description: You state £5/month revenue and ~£2 compute cost per generated video with an average of 20 videos/user/month. That implies ~£40/month compute cost per user against only £5 revenue — a ~£35/month loss per active user before any other costs. This single contradiction makes the stated business model financially impossible as written.
flaws.question: Which of these three numbers is wrong — price (£5), cost per video (£2), or average usage (20 videos/mo) — and what validated evidence supports the corrected figure?

flaws.title: No evidence users will pay £5 for unlimited generation
flaws.description: The plan asserts a £5 price but provides no demand evidence, price sensitivity testing, or willingness-to-pay research. At the declared price you must show why customers would choose unlimited access rather than a metered model or competitors. Without customer willingness-to-pay validated, the revenue side is purely speculative.
flaws.question: How did you determine customers will actually pay £5/month for unlimited video generation — show survey/experiment/conversion data or an MVP test plan?

flaws.title: No CAC, channels, or realistic acquisition plan at this price point
flaws.description: The document names no acquisition channels or expected CAC. Given the negative per-user margin even before CAC, you need channels that cost near-zero or convert virally — claims of 'viral growth' are unproven. Paid channels that produce paying users at scale are unlikely to be profitable at £5/month unless CAC is extremely low, which is unsubstantiated here.
flaws.question: What acquisition channels will you use and what is the measured or projected CAC per paying customer (with supporting tests or benchmarks)?

flaws.title: Key per-user costs beyond compute are omitted
flaws.description: Only compute cost per generated video is listed. There is no accounting for storage (raw/generated video), CDN/bandwidth, encoding/transcoding, backups, or per-user database costs. These recurring costs (particularly for video) can be material and will further worsen an already negative margin.
flaws.question: Provide estimates for per-user monthly storage, CDN/bandwidth, encoding, and other infra costs (not just compute per generation) or explain why they are negligible.

flaws.title: Payback period and CAC recovery not specified and likely impossible
flaws.description: With stated revenue and compute costs, gross margin is massively negative so any CAC will never be recovered. No payback period, LTV, churn, or CAC numbers are provided, so it's impossible to model unit economics over time. The business cannot scale if CAC cannot be paid back in a finite time.
flaws.question: Show a one-line LTV = revenue - direct costs calculation and a CAD (CAC) payback analysis — how long to recover CAC given your current numbers?

flaws.title: Hidden/operational costs (support, moderation, refunds, fraud, compliance) unaccounted
flaws.description: There is no mention of support staffing, content moderation, legal/compliance costs, chargebacks/refunds or fraud prevention. For a video generation platform these can be non-trivial, especially as usage and content variety scale, and will further erode margins if not planned for.
flaws.question: List expected operational costs per active user (support, moderation, payments/chargebacks, compliance) or show tests estimating their magnitude.

adversarial_competitor.summary: This plan sells "unlimited" AI video generation at £5/month while stating a ~£2 cost per generated video and an average of 20 videos/month — a straight loss-making proposition and an open invitation for incumbents to crush. The product has no stated defensible differentiation, no acquisition plan, and no demand evidence; a well-funded competitor can cheaply replicate or out-distribute and out-price it. Below are concrete weak points to exploit and the single sharp questions the founder must answer.

flaws.title: Negative unit economics: £5 revenue vs ~£40 expected cost
flaws.description: You claim £5/month price, ~£2 cost per video, and 20 videos/month per user — implying ~£40 cost per subscriber versus £5 revenue. That math makes the business model impossible as stated and is fatal unless costs, limits, or pricing change. A competitor can simply wait for burn or force price changes by offering temporary subsidies and then leverage scale.
flaws.question: How do you reconcile the stated £5/month price with a ~£2 per-video cost and an expected 20 videos/month (i.e., where does the ~£35 loss per user come from)?

flaws.title: No defensible differentiation — trivial to copy
flaws.description: The offering is described only by price and usage; there's no unique model, IP, dataset, or UX that prevents replication. With modest engineering, an incumbent can integrate their existing models or cloud discounts and match features or price quickly. Without a lock-in asset, the startup is commoditized and can be neutralized by feature parity plus distribution.
flaws.question: What unique asset (proprietary model, dataset, patent, exclusive partner, or distribution lock) prevents an incumbent from reproducing your service quickly?

flaws.title: Acquisition channel unspecified — incumbents can preempt distribution
flaws.description: No customer acquisition or go-to-market plan is given. Large competitors can push the same capability through existing channels (email lists, in-app prompts, bundled subscriptions, app stores, SEO) and capture demand before you build momentum. Your ability to reach users is the decisive battleground here.
flaws.question: How will you acquire customers cheaply at scale, and why can't incumbents block those channels or out-spend you to capture them first?

flaws.title: Pricing is easily weaponizable by incumbents
flaws.description: A well-funded competitor can neutralize your price advantage by bundling video generation into existing subscriptions, offering limited free tiers, or temporarily subsidizing usage to starve you of customers. You offer no lock or margin buffer to withstand predatory or bundled pricing moves from incumbents.
flaws.question: How will you defend a £5/month price against incumbents who can bundle, subsidize, or temporarily undercut you to protect their user base?

flaws.title: No evidence users will create 20 videos/month or pay for "unlimited"
flaws.description: The plan assumes heavy usage (20 videos/month) and willingness-to-pay for unlimited access without any demand testing. If actual usage or willingness-to-pay is lower, the unit economics change but if higher, losses worsen. This is an unvalidated behavioral assumption that incumbents can quickly test and exploit.
flaws.question: What evidence do you have that target users will both generate ~20 videos/month and pay £5 for unlimited access?

execution_risk.summary: The plan has a fatal internal contradiction between price and stated cost that prevents the product from being operable as described. Beyond that, the founder has not validated core inputs (per-video cost, user usage) nor addressed immediate blockers to shipping: legal/moderation requirements, infra/ops complexity, sequencing (abuse/quotas), or any go-to-market plan. Each of these gaps will prevent a safe, launchable product unless resolved before wider development.

flaws.title: Pricing vs stated cost makes the product impossible to operate as described
flaws.description: You promise £5/month for unlimited video generation while claiming ~£2 compute cost per generated video and 20 videos/month per user. That implies ~£40 in compute cost per subscriber against £5 revenue — the service as priced cannot be paid for and therefore cannot be shipped at scale. This is an internal contradiction that must be resolved before any engineering work continues, because it determines everything from infrastructure budget to acquisition strategy.
flaws.question: Which of these three numbers is wrong (price, £2/video cost, or 20 videos/user) — and how will you fund the resulting per-user loss while you build?

flaws.title: No empirical validation of usage or cost assumptions before building
flaws.description: You treat 20 videos/month and £2/video as facts but provide no evidence or test plan. Building full product, infra and billing on these untested numbers risks delivering a system that immediately bleeds money or doesn't meet user needs. The correct sequence is a small experiment to measure real per-video compute cost at your target fidelity and to observe real user generation behavior.
flaws.question: What is your cheapest, time-boxed experiment to validate both real per-video compute cost at target quality and how many videos a typical user will generate in a month?

flaws.title: No plan for content-moderation, legal or regulatory blockers (deepfakes, copyright)
flaws.description: Unlimited video generation is a high-risk content product: deepfakes, copyrighted source material, defamation and age-related restrictions can create immediate legal exposure, payment processor blocks, or platform delistings. You haven't specified policies, detection systems, consent/rights flow, or a takedown/legal process — leaving shipping likely to be blocked by third parties or to create customer-facing takedowns.
flaws.question: How will you prevent, detect, and legally handle disallowed or infringing generated content (e.g., deepfakes, copyrighted inputs) before offering unrestricted generation to subscribers?

flaws.title: Underestimated infrastructure and ops complexity for 'unlimited' video generation
flaws.description: An unlimited offering requires orchestration of heavy ML inference, GPU autoscaling, cost controls, video transcoding, storage (hot/cold) and CDN distribution plus monitoring and observability. The doc has no team plan, vendor choices, or runbooks; building these pieces is non-trivial and will take months and experienced SRE/ML engineers, not a few weeks.
flaws.question: Who on the team will provision and operate GPU fleets, autoscaling, storage and monitoring, and what is your minimal infra design and ETA to run 100 concurrent video jobs safely?

flaws.title: No distribution or customer-acquisition plan to actually get paying users
flaws.description: You state a price but provide no channel, cost-per-acquisition estimate, or launch plan. Without a validated acquisition funnel you will build a product that has no tested way to reach customers or to prove demand, and you won't be able to stress-test costs with real users.
flaws.question: What is the first paid or organic channel you will use to acquire subscribers and how will you measure its cost-effectiveness before a broader launch?

flaws.title: Sequencing risk: offering 'unlimited' before building throttles, billing controls and anti-abuse
flaws.description: Launching an unlimited plan without usage metering, fraud detection, rate-limits or emergency caps invites immediate abuse or runaway bills from a small number of users. The product should be shipped gated (invite/pilot), with hard quotas and monitoring, then relaxed once behavior and costs are understood.
flaws.question: What minimal throttles, monitoring and emergency-cost cutoffs will you implement for launch to prevent a small cohort from creating catastrophic costs?

pre_mortem.summary: The strategy rests on several unvalidated, high-leverage assumptions about user behavior, cost-per-video, and willingness to accept an unlimited £5/month plan. The single most likely cause of failure is that revealed usage patterns (frequency and intensity) diverged sharply from the stated 20 videos/month average, breaking the model. Several dependencies—cheaper compute or partnerships, a clearly identified buyer, and evidence users prefer unlimited vs. per-unit pricing—were never proven. First tests should validate who the buyer is, how often they will actually generate videos, and whether they prefer unlimited pricing before any build-out.

flaws.title: Unvalidated usage-intensity assumption (20 videos/month)
flaws.description: The plan hinges on an average subscriber creating 20 videos per month, but no evidence, survey data, or behavior-based estimate is provided. If real users generate more (or fewer) videos, both cost exposure and perceived value change dramatically. This single assumption directly determines platform sustainability and was never tested.
flaws.question: Who will generate how many videos per month in practice — what does early revealed-behavior testing show?

flaws.title: Assumed compute cost of ~£2/video is unproven and treated as fixed
flaws.description: The strategy states each generated video costs approx £2 but provides no sourcing, sensitivity, or contingency if that number changes. The plan implicitly assumes that cost-per-video will remain stable or fall, which is a high-dependency claim. If that cost is higher, volatile, or varies by video type/length, the model's assumptions about feasibility break down.
flaws.question: What is the empirical distribution of actual compute costs per produced video (by resolution/length/model), and how sensitive is the plan to increases there?

flaws.title: Assumes users prefer an unlimited £5/month model without demand testing
flaws.description: The founder chose unlimited access at a single low price but provides no evidence this matches user willingness-to-pay or purchasing behavior. Customers often prefer credits, tiers, or pay-as-you-go for high-variance consumption; the team conflated a low stated price with revealed adoption. If buyers value predictability or need higher quality outputs, they may reject or abuse an unlimited plan.
flaws.question: Do target customers choose unlimited monthly access at £5 in revealed choice tests, or do they prefer per-video/credit/tiered pricing?

flaws.title: Implicit dependency on cost-reduction or partner deals was unstated and unvalidated
flaws.description: Maintaining unlimited generation implies either sustained low compute costs or partner subsidies, yet no partnerships, supplier commitments, or roadmap for model efficiency were specified. The strategy assumes external conditions (hardware pricing, model efficiency) will remain favorable, a dependency that may not materialize within 18 months. Without proven channels to lower or stabilize costs, the business model is brittle.
flaws.question: What specific cost-reduction or partnership paths are guaranteed or realistically achievable within the 18-month horizon?

flaws.title: Target buyer is unspecified — who values unlimited, cheap AI video?
flaws.description: The document never defines whether the product targets hobbyists, creators, marketers, enterprises, or developers. Different buyer segments have dramatically different usage patterns, willingness to pay, and quality requirements, so conflating them is risky. Without a clear buyer, assumptions about average usage and pricing are unfounded.
flaws.question: Which specific customer segment is the primary buyer and what evidence shows they will adopt an unlimited £5/month service?

flaws.title: No evidence on alternatives or why customers would choose unlimited over current solutions
flaws.description: The plan doesn't describe what customers use today (manual production, other AI tools, agencies) or why they would switch to low-cost unlimited generation. This is a misread risk: customers might value higher fidelity, brand safety, or editing control more than volume, so unlimited low-cost generation may not be compelling. The lack of differentiation validation means demand may be weaker than assumed.
flaws.question: What current solutions do target users actually use, and why would they abandon them for unlimited low-cost AI video?

evidence_audit.summary: Evidence base: Weak. The document is pre-launch and provides no measured pilots, benchmarks or sourcing for price, cost-per-video, or usage. Most importantly, the stated numbers create an arithmetic contradiction that makes unit economics negative unless one or more inputs are changed and evidenced.

flaws.title: Unit economics are impossible: £5 revenue vs £40 cost per user
flaws.description: At the stated inputs the plan loses money on every subscriber: revenue £5/month versus cost = 20 videos × £2 = £40/month, so contribution margin = £5 − £40 = −£35/user-month. This single arithmetic contradiction breaks the whole plan unless one of the core numbers (price, cost per video, or usage) is changed and evidenced. The document gives no measured data, pilot or scenario that resolves this gap.
flaws.question: Show the concrete scenario that yields non-negative contribution margin at £5/mo by providing the measured cost-per-video and measured (or pilot-validated) average videos/month such that 5 ≥ cost_per_video × avg_videos.

flaws.title: Claimed ~£2 per generated video is unsourced and incompatible with price
flaws.description: The document asserts ~£2 compute cost per video but provides no breakdown, benchmark or measurement. For the £5/mo unlimited price to be viable at the claimed 20 videos/month the per-video cost must be ≤£0.25 (5/20), so £2 is an order of magnitude too high. Without a cost model or evidence of dramatic cost-reduction, the £2 figure undermines feasibility.
flaws.question: Provide a detailed cost breakdown and supporting measurements that justify the ~£2 per-video figure, and if you intend to keep £5/mo show a credible plan (with numbers) to reduce cost per video to ≤£0.25.

flaws.title: Average usage assumption (20 videos/month) is load-bearing and unsupported
flaws.description: Average videos/user of 20/month is central: it multiplies into compute costs and determines break-even. No survey, pilot, or comparable benchmark is provided. Given current pricing and claimed costs, break-even requires average usage ≤2.5 videos/month (5/2), so the assumed 20× is incompatible with any positive margin without other changes.
flaws.question: Provide evidence (pilot data, surveys, or benchmarks) that average subscribers will generate 20 videos/month, or state the empirically supported average and show the resulting contribution margin at £5/mo.

flaws.title: Pricing (£5 unlimited) has no customer willingness-to-pay evidence
flaws.description: The plan sets a customer-facing price and unlimited usage but offers no evidence customers would pay £5 for unlimited AI video generation. Willingness-to-pay, perceived value, and competitive alternatives determine whether users accept this price; none are cited. Pricing without demand evidence could lead to a mismatch between assumed subscriber numbers and reality.
flaws.question: Share evidence that customers will pay £5/mo for unlimited video generation (e.g. surveys, landing-page signups with price, preorders, or paid pilot results).

flaws.title: No acquisition/CAC inputs provided to validate scale or LTV assumptions
flaws.description: The document lacks any acquisition plan or CAC estimate, so there's no way to assess whether subscribers can be acquired at a cost that makes the (already-negative) unit economics remotely recoverable via lifetime value. Even an idea-stage product must show a plausible path to acquiring users at a sustainable cost.
flaws.question: Provide expected CAC with supporting data (pilot campaign results, channel benchmarks, or landing-page conversion rates) and show how CAC compares to customer lifetime contribution given your price and cost assumptions.

With basic feature parity (a free or low-cost scheduling tier), leverage of existing distribution (SEO, app stores, partner channels) and aggressive promotional pricing, a competitor can replicate or absorb these customers quickly. The founder must prove a moat, validated scalable acquisition channels, and unit economics to survive that pressure.

flaws.title: No defensible product differentiation or moat
flaws.description: The document states only price and current MRR but describes no unique feature, IP, integrations, network effects or service that would prevent incumbents from copying the product. With no visible technical or go-to-market barrier, a well-funded competitor can add an equivalent scheduling feature or bundle it into an existing suite within months. This makes the product vulnerable to rapid neutralization through feature parity or acquisition.
flaws.question: What specific, hard-to-copy feature, integration, or network effect prevents a competitor from reproducing your core value in 2–3 months?

flaws.title: Go-to-market plan is under-specified and easily outpaced
flaws.description: Acquisition is described only as 'referrals and partnerships with fitness instructors' with no validated channels, funnels, or growth metrics. execution_risk.summary: The plan asserts a near-perfect predictive model and a paid retail subscription with no data, team, compliance or go-to-market details. The biggest shipping risks are regulatory blocking (selling trading predictions to retail can be regulated), lack of any data/validation for the 95% accuracy claim, and a severe underestimation of engineering, ML and compliance effort. Smaller but real risks are wrong sequencing (selling before validating), no customer acquisition plan, and an untested price point.

flaws.title: Regulatory/financial-advice blocker — selling predictions may be regulated as investment advice
flaws.description: Offering a model that predicts stock movements to retail users likely falls into financial advice / investment product territory in many jurisdictions. Without a compliance plan the project can trigger cease-and-desist orders, fines, or mandatory registration as an advisor or broker—any of which would block or dramatically change the business model. The document contains no legal or jurisdictional analysis or plan for licensed distribution.
flaws.question: Which jurisdictions and regulators (e.g., SEC, FCA or equivalent) have you reviewed, and what licenses, registrations, or compliance processes are required to sell predictive stock signals to retail users there?

flaws.title: No data or validation plan — the 95% accuracy claim is ungrounded
flaws.description: You have neither collected data nor run experiments yet claim 95% accuracy. Failure mode: spending months building product and infra only to find no accessible data, label quality problems, or that the model cannot reach anywhere near that accuracy on out-of-sample tests. There is no minimal dataset, backtest plan, or falsification metric documented.
flaws.question: What minimum historical and live data will you need, how will you access it, and what exact backtest/out-of-sample metric would falsify the '95% accuracy' claim?

flaws.title: Underestimated engineering, ML and ops scope — team/timeline mismatch
flaws.description: Delivering a production-grade financial ML product requires data ingestion pipelines, feature engineering, label generation, backtesting framework, model monitoring, latency-sensitive infra, security, billing and UX. The idea-stage plan implies rapid execution but contains no team, roles or timeline; failure mode: a tiny team spends months and still ships a brittle MVP with no monitoring or reproducibility.
flaws.question: Who is on the team (engineers, ML researchers, quant traders, ops), and what is a realistic timeline and milestone plan for data pipelines, model validation, production infra, and monitoring?

flaws.title: Sequencing error — building subscriptions before proving predictive value
flaws.description: You plan to sell subscriptions at $49/month without first validating the core hypothesis that the model produces reliable, tradeable signals. Failure mode: customers sign up briefly then churn when predictions fail, or legal/ethical issues arise from wrong signals. The cheapest missing step (backtests, simulated/paper trading) is not described.
flaws.question: What is the minimum validation experiment (backtest, paper-trade period, or pilot) you will run and what pass/fail criteria will you require before opening paid subscriptions?

flaws.title: No acquisition or trust-building plan for retail traders
flaws.description: There is no go-to-market plan: no channels, partners, influencer strategy, trials, or trust mechanisms (proof-of-performance, third-party audits). Failure mode: a built product with near-zero traction because retail traders distrust black-box claims and acquisition costs are far higher than assumed.
flaws.question: Which specific acquisition channels and trust-building tactics (e.g., audits, paper-trade demos, partnerships with brokers) will you use, and what are your CAC/lead assumptions to reach initial users?

flaws.title: Pricing untested — $49/mo is arbitrary
flaws.description: $49/month is asserted without evidence of willingness-to-pay, trial structure, or competitive benchmarking. Failure mode: price too high to attract skeptical retail traders or too low to cover compliance and infra, causing poor retention or unprofitable unit economics.
flaws.question: How will you test willingness-to-pay (pilot pricing, trials, freemium) and what conversion or retention thresholds will validate the $49/mo price?

pre_mortem.summary: The plan rests on an extraordinary, untested technical claim (95% predictive accuracy) and multiple unstated assumptions about data, model generalization, and customer willingness to pay. If any of those central assumptions fail, the product has no foundation. The highest-risk items are the accuracy claim itself, the availability of usable data that generalizes, and the unvalidated assumption that retail traders will subscribe without a vetted track record or trust signals.

flaws.title: Core claim of 95% predictive accuracy is unsubstantiated and implausible
flaws.description: The strategy's single foundational claim is that an AI model can predict stock-market movements with 95% accuracy; the document provides no data, experiments, or definition of the metric. This claim must be true for the business to exist as stated; if it is false or never demonstrated on realistic, out-of-sample data, the entire plan collapses. No alternative business model is described if this turns out to be unattainable.
flaws.question: What empirical, out-of-sample evidence (with a precise prediction horizon and label definition) demonstrates >=95% accuracy under realistic testing conditions?

flaws.title: No evidence retail traders will pay $49/month for this product
flaws.description: The $49/month price and the buyer (retail traders) are asserted without any demand validation. Retail traders typically require verifiable performance history, trust, integrations, or different packaging; assuming they'll subscribe to an unproven black-box model is a large leap. The plan lacks any stated experiments to validate willingness-to-pay or product-market fit.
flaws.question: Can you show validated willingness-to-pay (e.g., pre-sales, paid pilot commitments, or conversion on a landing page) from retail traders at $49/mo?

flaws.title: Assumes access to clean, exhaustive data and that models will generalize despite market non‑stationarity
flaws.description: No data collection plan or discussion of look-ahead bias, survivorship bias, regime shifts, or covariate shift is provided. The idea assumes training data exists and will produce a model that generalizes to live markets—an assumption that often fails for financial prediction problems. If suitable, unbiased historical data or a protocol to avoid overfitting does not materialize, the claimed performance is unachievable.
flaws.question: What exact datasets and validation protocols will you use to train and test the model, and do walk-forward/backtest results survive tests for look-ahead and regime-change biases?

flaws.title: Accuracy metric (95%) is not connected to real trader value or profitability
flaws.description: Even if direction predictions are 95% accurate by some definition, that metric may not translate into profitable, usable signals after accounting for timing, position sizing, slippage, and transaction costs. The founder hasn't specified prediction granularity (next tick, day, week) or how accuracy maps to net P&L for retail traders. This mismatch could mean the marketed metric is irrelevant to customers.
flaws.question: How does your chosen accuracy metric (horizon, label, frequency) convert into net trader P&L after realistic costs and execution constraints?

flaws.title: Misread of trust/ differentiation: retail traders may require audited track record or explainability
flaws.description: The plan assumes retail traders will adopt and pay for access to a predictive AI model without articulating trust-building features (verified track record, audited performance, explainability, or integration with broker platforms). It also does not state why traders would choose this offering over existing signal providers, copy-trading, or broker tools. This is a gap in understanding the buyer's selection criteria.
flaws.question: What evidence or product features (e.g., audited returns, explainability, broker integrations) will differentiate your product and convince retail traders to trust and buy it?

flaws.title: Regulatory/operational assumption: ability to sell market predictions without advice/licensing constraints
flaws.description: The document assumes the product can be sold directly to retail traders as a subscription without addressing whether providing predictive signals constitutes regulated investment advice in target jurisdictions. If the offering requires licensing or adherence to disclosure rules, that will materially change go-to-market and trust requirements. No legal/regulatory validation is described.
flaws.question: Have you validated the legal/regulatory classification of selling market predictions in your initial target markets and what restrictions or disclosures will be required?

evidence_audit.summary: Evidence base: Weak. The plan is purely conceptual with no data, experiments, or customers. The most important gap is the complete absence of any out-of-sample evaluation or data-backed evidence for the 95% accuracy claim.

flaws.title: 95% accuracy claim is entirely unsupported
flaws.description: You state the model will achieve 95% accuracy but have no data, backtest, pilot or experiment. This single number is the core technical claim and cannot be accepted without an out-of-sample evaluation showing how accuracy was measured, what data and period were used, and how results generalise. Without that evidence the central technical premise of the plan is unproven and could be false.
flaws.question: Provide a concrete out-of-sample evaluation (dataset, time period, train/test split method, exact prediction task, and resulting confusion matrix or equivalent) that demonstrates 95% accuracy under realistic conditions.

flaws.title: Prediction target and metric are undefined (makes 95% meaningless)
flaws.description: You don't define what 'predicts stock-market movements' or '95% accuracy' mean: direction vs magnitude, time horizon (next tick, day, month), the unit of prediction, class balance, or whether accuracy is compared to a baseline. These definitions determine whether 95% is trivial (e.g. always predict the majority class) or genuinely predictive.
flaws.question: Specify the exact prediction target (asset universe, forecasting horizon, frequency), the positive class definition, the metric(s) you will report (accuracy, precision/recall, Sharpe, P&L after costs), and the baseline accuracy to beat.

flaws.title: No data acquisition / dataset plan described
flaws.description: You haven't stated which historical market data, features, labels, or alternative datasets you'll use, nor their availability, cost, latency or licensing. Success depends on having suitable, high-quality data for training and realistic backtesting; without it the modelling claim is hollow.
flaws.question: Provide the specific data sources you will use (vendors/APIs, fields, time span, sample size), their costs/licensing terms, and a plan for obtaining cleaned, timestamped data suitable for backtesting.
