The most important outstanding issue is the lack of any measured accuracy or willingness-to-pay / acquisition evidence to support the 95% accuracy claim and $49/month revenue model.

flaws.title: 95% prediction accuracy is a load‑bearing unsourced number
flaws.description: The central technical claim — a model that predicts stock-market movements with 95% accuracy — is stated as a target with no data, backtest, experiment or method. This number is the foundation for pricing and demand but currently has no provenance (dataset, time period, out-of-sample performance or evaluation metric). Without measured results the plan has no bridge from concept to product-market fit.
flaws.question: Provide measured performance: a reproducible evaluation (dataset description, time range, sample size, train/holdout split and the model's out-of-sample accuracy and relevant metrics) showing performance close to 95%; if unavailable, state the largest empirical accuracy achieved and on what data.

flaws.title: No evidence retail traders want or will use this
flaws.description: Founder admits to zero conversations with retail traders and gives no market discovery data. Demand for a high‑accuracy trading predictor is not self-evident; willingness to pay, use patterns, and trust thresholds among retail traders are unknown. This makes revenue and growth projections (implicit in selling subscriptions) unsupported.
flaws.question: Share customer discovery evidence: results from structured interviews or surveys with a specified number of retail traders (n) showing the fraction who would pay for this product, how they would use it, and the stated maximum monthly price.

flaws.title: Price point ($49/mo) is asserted without willingness‑to‑pay evidence
flaws.description: The $49 monthly price is presented as the revenue model but has no supporting data showing retail traders will pay that amount for this type of signal or service. Price interacts with conversion, churn and LTV; without tests the revenue model is speculative.
flaws.question: Provide evidence that $49/month is acceptable: results from pricing experiments, surveys with explicit price choice, or conversion estimates from a landing‑page test at that price and the sample size used.

flaws.title: No customer acquisition plan or CAC / funnel assumptions
flaws.description: The document contains no channels, experiments or cost assumptions for acquiring retail subscribers. Without at least an initial measured CAC or validated channel, you cannot project how many signups $X spend will produce or whether the unit economics support the price point.
flaws.question: Specify initial acquisition channel(s) and provide measured or conservatively bounded CAC (with source) and an expected conversion funnel (impressions → leads → paid) for each channel.

flaws.title: Buyer segment is underspecified — who exactly is the paying customer?
flaws.description: The target is loosely described as 'retail traders' but there is no segmentation (day traders vs. long-term retail, geographic or regulatory constraints, platform preferences). Different retail segments will have different price sensitivity and use cases, which affects demand and acquisition strategy.
flaws.question: Define the paying customer precisely: which retail trader segment(s) you target first, with rationale and any evidence that this segment would value a predictive signal enough to subscribe.

pre_mortem.summary: The plan rests on a single extraordinary technical claim (95% predictive accuracy) with no supporting evidence and no customer discovery. Key assumptions about who will pay, what metric matters to users, and access to suitable data were unstated and thus likely false. The most probable failure is that the model never achieves robust, out-of-sample predictive performance that actually matters to retail traders.

flaws.title: Core technical claim (95% accuracy) is unsupported and likely unattainable in real markets
flaws.description: The founder states a 95% accuracy target but has no data, experiments, or definition of the metric. Financial markets are noisy and non-stationary; without out-of-sample live-forward evidence, the 95% figure is a hypothesis, not a capability. If the model cannot deliver predictive performance prospectively, the product value disappears instantly.
flaws.question: What live, out-of-sample evidence can you produce (forward test, not backtest) that your model achieves the claimed accuracy on future market data?

flaws.title: No customer discovery — buyer persona is unknown
flaws.description: The founder has not spoken to any retail traders and therefore has not validated who the customer actually is, what their workflow is, or whether they would accept a $49/mo subscription. Without identifying specific paying personas (active day traders, swing traders, novices), the product could be misaligned with actual needs and distribution channels.
flaws.question: Which specific retail trader persona is the first paying customer and what primary evidence (interviews, commitments, paid trials) shows they want this product?

flaws.title: Pricing and willingness-to-pay are assumed, not tested
flaws.description: The $49/month price is asserted with no validation of willingness to pay, elasticity, or alternative commercial models. Different segments of retail traders have very different value perceptions and budgets; treating $49 as a given risks building a product no one will convert to pay for.
flaws.question: What direct evidence (pre-sales, pricing experiments, competitor pricing comparisons with conversion data) shows retail traders will pay $49/month for your offering?

flaws.title: Metric mismatch: accuracy ≠ trader value (profitability/utility not defined)
flaws.description: The plan focuses on a single accuracy number without specifying what 'accuracy' means (directional, magnitude, time horizon) or showing that that metric correlates with trader outcomes (profit, risk-adjusted return, reduced drawdown). High nominal accuracy can coincide with no economic benefit to users if it's concentrated on low-impact signals.
flaws.question: Which specific, business-relevant performance metric (e.g., risk-adjusted return per trade, hit rate on high-conviction signals) will you optimize, and how do you prove it improves traders' outcomes in realistic tests?

flaws.title: Unstated dependency on access to suitable, high-quality market data
flaws.description: No datasets, frequency, time horizon, or labeling approach are specified; the founder has not tested that the necessary historical and live data are obtainable or fit for training a production-grade predictive model. If the data needed are expensive, restricted, or insufficiently rich, model development will stall or overfit.
flaws.question: What exact datasets (symbols, time resolution, history length) will you use for training and validation, and can you practically obtain them under realistic cost and licensing constraints?

execution_risk.summary: The plan lists price, a monthly acquisition target, a daily marketing spend and a 2-year lifetime, but key inputs and operational details are missing. The biggest shipping risks are legal/regulatory obligations around handling resumes (PII), unproven acquisition math (currency/CAC missing), an unsupported willingness-to-pay assumption for graduates at $800/year, and substantial technical work to build a defensible AI reviewer without any data or model plan. Also missing: a validated go-to-market/channel sequence and any team/timeline, which together make delivery and early growth likely to fail or be much slower than implied.

flaws.title: No data-privacy / PII compliance plan for handling resumes (possible regulatory shutdown)
flaws.description: Resumes contain personal and sensitive data; the document has no geography, consent flows, retention policy, security, GDPR/CCPA considerations, or plan for legal counsel. Shipping without compliance risks fines, forced data deletion, or being blocked by cloud providers or enterprise customers. This is a show-stopper for any meaningful user acquisition or onboarding in regulated markets.
flaws.question: In which jurisdictions will you operate and how will you legally collect, store, process, and delete applicant PII (consent, data retention, DSRs, security controls) before you accept real resumes?

flaws.title: Acquisition math is unusable: currency, CAC and channel details missing
flaws.description: You state $/800 per year, 25 customers/month and 20 per day marketing spend but didn’t specify currency or conversion assumptions, acquisition channels, conversion rates, or customer funnel. Without currency and CAC estimates you can't tell whether 20/day is adequate or whether 25 customers/month is reachable — this will lead to an underfunded launch or wrong marketing experiments.
flaws.question: What currency are you using, what channels and conversion rates produce 25 customers/month, and what CAC do you expect from 20 (units)/day of marketing spend?

flaws.title: Price (800/year) is unsupported for 'graduates' — no evidence graduates will pay
flaws.description: Charging 800/year to recent graduates is a strong assumption with no validation: no willingness-to-pay tests, no segmentation (senior vs fresh grads), and no alternative payment options (one-off review, freemium). If graduates won’t pay that price the product will need a different monetization or customer segment.
flaws.question: Who exactly is the paying customer (which graduate segment and geography) and what evidence (surveys, preorders, paid pilots) do you have that they will pay 800/year?

flaws.title: No data/model plan: building reliable AI CV review requires labelled data and bias controls
flaws.description: An ML-driven CV reviewer needs training/evaluation datasets, a rubric, and bias mitigation; none of this is described. Failure modes include producing low-quality or discriminatory advice, high false positives/negatives, or unpredictable outputs that harm users and reputation. Without a plan to obtain labeled resumes and human QA, the product will be brittle at launch.
flaws.question: What labeled data, human-review process, and fairness/QA checks will you use to train and validate the CV reviewer before onboarding paying users?

flaws.title: Sequencing risk: building platform before validating acquisition or willingness to pay
flaws.description: The document implies product development is underway but contains no plan to validate channels, pricing, or target conversion before full build. If you complete the product first and only then discover CAC or price are wrong, you’ll waste months of engineering effort and miss a fast pivot window.
flaws.question: What is your minimum viable test (landing page, preorders, concierge reviews) to validate you can acquire paying graduates at target CAC before building the full product?

flaws.title: No team, timeline, or operational plan — scope likely underestimated
flaws.description: There is no stated team size, roles, or timeline. Building a reliable AI reviewer, UX for CV uploads, secure storage, billing, and onboarding 25 paying customers/month plus support is nontrivial; without resourcing the project will slip, burn out founders, or launch incomplete.
flaws.question: Who is building and operating the product (engineers, ML, legal, customer support) and what timeline and milestones show you can deliver the MVP and handle 25 paying customers/month?

adversarial_competitor.summary: This concept is highly attackable: the founder proposes an AI CV-review for graduates at $800/yr with no validation, unclear customer target, and a vague acquisition plan. A well-funded incumbent can neutralize it cheaply by bundling a free/basic AI review into an existing product, undercutting pricing, and using existing distribution (SEO, app store, email lists, partnerships) to capture early users before the startup launches.

flaws.title: No evidence graduates will pay $800/year (price + demand unvalidated)
flaws.description: The plan names a price (800/yr) but provides no evidence that graduates will pay that amount or who actually pays (student, parents, schools, employers). At this price point the product is either a premium or enterprise offering — a mismatch vs the 'graduates' buyer implied. This is fatal because a competitor can offer a free/basic alternative and win adoption while the startup struggles to convert.
flaws.question: What validated evidence (surveys with willingness-to-pay, paid pilots, or signed letters of intent) shows a material cohort of graduates will pay 800/year for this service?

flaws.title: Differentiation is undefined and trivially copyable
flaws.description: No unique features, exclusive data, or barriers to replication are stated. Automated CV feedback is a commodity ML use-case: incumbents or platforms with large user bases can add a similar model + UX and absorb the market. Without a clear defensible moat (unique training data, partnerships with universities/employers, or placement guarantees), the product is easy to neutralize.
flaws.question: What concrete, defensible features or exclusive data/partnerships prevent an incumbent from shipping a functionally equivalent CV-review in weeks?

flaws.title: Acquisition plan and unit economics are incoherent
flaws.description: They target 25 customers/month with marketing '20 per day' (currency not set) and no channel strategy. There is no CAC, conversion funnel, nor channels listed (SEO, partnerships, campus outreach). A well-funded competitor can exploit this by using existing channels and much lower incremental CAC to procure users at scale before the startup finds a repeatable funnel.
flaws.question: Which specific channels and measured conversion rates produce 25 customers/month and what is the true CAC in a real currency?

flaws.title: Unclear buyer segmentation — 'graduates' is too broad
flaws.description: The target is simply 'graduates' with no segmentation (recent grads, students, geography, discipline). Different buyer segments have very different willingness-to-pay and acquisition costs. Without a prioritized buyer persona, the product cannot focus messaging, partnerships, or pricing — enabling incumbents to pick the most valuable segments and dominate them first.
flaws.question: Which exact graduate segment (age, schooling, region, discipline) is the initial target and why will that segment convert at the proposed price?

flaws.title: Key numbers are incomplete and contradictory (marketing cost currency missing)
flaws.description: Marketing cost is stated as '20 per day' with no currency, and lifetime is given as 2 years but no churn, ARPU, or CAC are provided. These missing inputs prevent even a basic unit-economics test and let competitors undercut using predictable pricing and subsidies.
flaws.question: Supply the missing unit-economics: currency for marketing cost, expected CAC, conversion rates, ARPU, and churn assumptions that lead to sustainable LTV/CAC.

unit_economics.summary: The doc lists price (800/year), a 25 new customers/month target, marketing spend (20/day) and a 2-year average lifetime, but omits currency and every cost input needed to compute unit economics. With missing CAC by channel, cost-to-serve (compute, storage, support, payment fees) and no evidence of willingness-to-pay, you cannot calculate gross margin or payback. First tests: run a small paid-acquisition experiment to measure CPA and a pricing test (landing page / paid pilots) to validate willingness-to-pay before building more product.

flaws.title: Currency and core unit inputs are undefined — math is unanchored
flaws.description: You gave price (800/yr) and marketing (20/day) but explicitly 'haven't chosen a currency yet.' Without a currency and consistent units you cannot compute CAC, ARPU, LTV in meaningful terms or compare costs to revenue. This makes every downstream metric (payback, margin) impossible to verify.
flaws.question: What currency are you using and please restate price, marketing spend and all per-period amounts in that currency?

flaws.title: Willingness-to-pay is unsupported — 800/yr is an unvalidated hypothesis
flaws.description: The plan assumes customers will pay 800 per year but provides no evidence (surveys, pilots, price experiments, or anchor customers). You haven't specified who actually pays (student, university, employer) or whether that group can and will pay 800/year. Revenue projections hinge entirely on this untested price.
flaws.question: Who is the paying customer and what concrete validation (paid pilots, preorders, pricing tests or survey results) supports charging 800/year?

flaws.title: CAC and acquisition channels are unspecified yet the target implies an unrealistic CPA
flaws.description: You target 25 customers/month and list 20/day marketing spend but don't name channels, expected conversion rates, or how spend maps to customers. Without channel-level CPAs you can't verify that 20/day can deliver 25 customers/month or what CAC will be, so the acquisition plan is unsupported by numbers.
flaws.question: Which acquisition channels will you use and what are your assumed channel-level conversion rates and resulting CACs to deliver 25 customers/month?

flaws.title: Cost to serve (compute, storage, support, payment processing) is missing
flaws.description: There is no per-user estimate for compute (AI inference cost), storage, support (human reviews/CS), or payment processing fees. For an AI CV review product, inference and storage could be material; without these unit costs you cannot estimate gross margin or determine if 800/yr yields attractive unit economics.
flaws.question: Provide per-customer monthly estimates for compute/inference, storage, customer support and payment processing fees so gross margin can be calculated.

flaws.title: Payback period and LTV/CAC math are undeclared and fragile
flaws.description: You state average lifetime = 2 years (implying LTV = 1,600 in your unit) but give no CAC or churn curve, so payback period cannot be calculated. If CAC is higher than assumed or if churn is front-loaded, payback could be far longer than the business can support, but the document contains no sensitivity or break-even analysis.
flaws.question: What is your projected CAC and monthly churn so we can compute LTV:CAC and payback period (in months)?

flaws.title: Hidden and operating costs (moderation, refunds, chargebacks, fraud, compliance) are ignored
flaws.description: No mention of moderation (AI output review), compliance (data/privacy for CVs), refund/chargeback rates, or fraud mitigation. These items can become significant operating costs or increase churn and payment losses, materially changing unit economics if unaccounted for.
flaws.question: Have you estimated potential costs for moderation/review, refunds/chargebacks and privacy/compliance work per customer, and what are those estimates?

pre_mortem.summary: The plan rests on several untested, high-leverage assumptions: that graduates will pay an annual fee of “800” (currency unspecified) for an ongoing AI CV review subscription, that a meaningful cohort will remain customers for two years, and that the team can acquire 25 customers/month with a daily marketing budget of “20.” The most likely killing blow is pricing/packaging mismatch: prospective users prefer free or one-off help and will not subscribe at the stated price, collapsing demand before launch. Core missing evidence: who exactly the buyer is, willingness-to-pay validation, and a concrete, channel-specific acquisition test.

flaws.title: Critical: Price and payment model (800/year) is unvalidated and likely mismatched to buyer willingness
flaws.description: You state a list price of 800 per year but give no currency, no rationale for annual billing, and no evidence that recent graduates will pay an ongoing subscription for CV reviews. Graduates are typically cash-constrained and often prefer one-off, outcome-driven purchases; assuming they will pay a recurring annual fee is a high-risk leap. If this assumption is wrong, the product never reaches steady traction.
flaws.question: What concrete evidence (preorders, paid trials, or willingness-to-pay tests) shows the target graduate cohort will purchase an annual subscription at 800 in a specified currency rather than use free/one-off options?

flaws.title: High: No evidence that graduates actually demand a paid AI CV review (stated vs revealed preference)
flaws.description: The document contains no user research, pilot results, or conversion data to support the core demand hypothesis. You may be confusing expressed interest in 'better CVs' with actual willingness to pay for an AI subscription. Without simple tests (landing page preorders, pricing A/B ads, or paid pilot offers), you won't know if the product solves a monetizable problem.
flaws.question: Can you show a minimal test (landing page with buy button, ad-driven signups with price shown, or paid pilot) that validates conversion at or near the proposed price?

flaws.title: High: 'Graduates' is too broad—the true buyer/payer is undefined
flaws.description: Labeling the customer as 'graduates' leaves huge ambiguity: Are you targeting final-year students, recent grads (<6 months), career switchers, or specific majors/regions? Different segments vary dramatically in budget, urgency, channels, and trust in AI. You also haven't specified who would pay (student, parent, employer, university). This ambiguity makes your pricing, acquisition, and retention assumptions ungrounded.
flaws.question: Which specific graduate segment (age, career stage, geography, field) will you target first, and who within that segment will actually pay for the service?

flaws.title: High: Customer lifetime = 2 years is an unsupported subscription assumption
flaws.description: Assuming an average customer stays for 2 years implies recurring, repeatable value after graduation. In reality, most graduates need CV help briefly at job search time; retention is likely low unless the product expands into ongoing career services. This overestimates lifetime and underestimates churn risk, biasing product and pricing choices toward subscription when a one-off or credit-based model might be the revealed preference.
flaws.question: Why do you expect customers to retain an annual subscription for two years instead of making a single, short-term purchase, and how will you test actual retention behavior cheaply?

flaws.title: Medium: Acquisition plan and the '20 per day' marketing budget are vague and untested
flaws.description: You state an acquisition target (25/month) and marketing cost (20/day) but neither currency nor channel is specified. There's no evidence these numbers map to realistic cost-per-acquisition in relevant channels (campus partnerships, social ads, Discord/Reddit, career fairs). If the assumed channel CACs are higher than implied, the target acquisition rate won't materialize.
flaws.question: Which specific marketing channels and audience-targeting tactics map the '20/day' budget to an expected cost-per-acquisition, and can you run a small, budgeted ad experiment to validate CAC?

flaws.title: Medium: No clear differentiation vs free tools, university services, or one-off human reviewers
flaws.description: The strategy assumes 'AI CV review' is a strong enough differentiator, but many free AI tools, university career centers, peer networks, and affordable human reviewers already serve graduates. You haven't specified what measurable outcome you deliver better (higher interview invite rate, vetted ATS optimization, recruiter feedback) that would justify the price and subscription model.
flaws.question: What specific outcome (e.g., X% higher interview rate, ATS pass rate, recruiter-validated score) do you deliver that free tools and current alternatives do not, and how will you prove it in a pilot?

evidence_audit.summary: Evidence base: Weak. The plan is pre-launch with no real revenue or customer traction; founder lists price, acquisition and spend targets but provides no measured conversion or pilot data. flaws.title: Currency for price and marketing spend is unspecified
flaws.description: The plan states a price of 800 per year and marketing at 20 per day but explicitly says no currency chosen. Without a currency, you cannot compute CAC, revenue, LTV or compare costs and price consistently. All derived economics in the document implicitly assume the same currency for both figures; that assumption is unstated and load-bearing.

flaws.title: Stated marketing spend implies implausibly low CAC and huge LTV:CAC unless justified
flaws.description: If marketing is 20/day → 20×30≈600 per month, and you plan 25 customers/month, implied CAC = 600/25 = 24. With price = 800/year and lifetime = 2 years, LTV = 800×2 = 1600, giving LTV:CAC ≈ 1600/24 ≈ 67 and payback ≈ 24/(800/12) ≈ 0.36 months. That is unusually attractive and therefore a red flag unless you can show conversion rates or channel evidence that produce CAC=24. This arithmetic assumes the same currency for price and ad spend (see previous flaw).
flaws.question: Provide measured conversion rates or a channel/campaign example showing that 20/day marketing spend produces 25 paid customers/month (or supply an expected CAC and its source); if you cannot, run a 30-day pilot at 20/day and report paid conversions.

flaws.title: Average customer lifetime (2 years) is unsupported and materially affects economics
flaws.description: You assert a 2-year average lifetime (implying ~50% annual churn) but give no basis. Lifetime drives LTV (LTV = price × lifetime = 1600 under current numbers) and therefore whether acquisition spend is sustainable. With 25 new customers/month (300/year) and churn = 50%/year, steady-state customer base = new_per_year / churn = 300/0.5 = 600 customers → implied steady revenue = 600×800 = 480,000 per year (assuming same currency).
flaws.question: Show the data or rationale for the 2-year lifetime (historical churn from pilots, comparable product benchmarks, or user-research evidence); if none, run a cohort churn measurement over three months and report monthly retention.

flaws.title: No demand evidence or pilot to support the 25 customers/month target
flaws.description: The target of 25 customers/month is a forecast with no reported experiments, waitlist, pilot conversions, or survey backing. At idea-stage this is expected, but the plan depends on this rate to claim unit-economics success; without a small test the target is just an assumption.
flaws.question: Run a low-cost pilot (e.g., a 30-day campaign at your stated 20/day spend and a simple landing page) and report paid conversions, cost per paid customer, and funnel conversion rates.

flaws.title: Ambiguous definition: are 25 customers/month gross acquisitions or net (after churn)?

adversarial_competitor.summary: You claim an AI condition-monitoring product selling $24k/year to large manufacturers and plan to sign 15 customers in three months, but you have two engineers, no sales team, and no pilots. This is a classic easy-to-neutralize startup: the core tech is incremental (anomaly detection), incumbent platforms can add it quickly, and well-funded competitors can use distribution, free pilots, aggressive pricing, and brand/trust to make your offering redundant before launch. Before you build, you must prove buyer demand, willing-to-pay, and a credible route to enterprise deals.

pre_mortem.summary: The strategy rests on unvalidated demand and multiple unstated go-to-market assumptions. The founder projects 15 $24k enterprise contracts in 3 months without any customer conversations, pilots, a sales plan, or clarity on the buyer — any one of which could collapse the plan. The most likely killing blow is simple: prospective manufacturers decline to commit to paid pilots or annual contracts because the team has not demonstrated value or secured access to operational data.

flaws.title: No demand evidence — zero customer conversations or pilots
flaws.description: The founder admits they have not spoken to any manufacturers and have no confirmed pilots, yet assumes immediate enterprise demand. Building a product for an unvalidated need (15 customers in 3 months) risks producing something nobody will buy. This is the foundational assumption: if customers don't want it, nothing else matters.
flaws.question: Which specific manufacturers have agreed to a pilot or purchase, and can you get at least one signed LOI or paid pilot before proceeding?

flaws.title: Pricing claim ($24k/year) is unsupported by buyer research
flaws.description: The plan states a $24k annual contract to 'large manufacturers' but the founder skipped 'who pays, and roughly how much'. There's no evidence that the relevant buyer (maintenance manager, operations, procurement) sees $24k as the right price or will accept subscription billing for this solution. If the assumed price is wrong, the commercial model and sales targets are invalid.
flaws.question: Who (exact role/title) will sign a $24k/year contract and have they confirmed willingness to pay that amount for this solution?

flaws.title: Unrealistic early customer target — ignores enterprise sales and pilot timelines
flaws.description: Targeting 15 enterprise customers within the first three months with two engineers and no sales staff presumes a short sales cycle and immediate readiness to buy. Large manufacturers typically require pilots, security reviews, legal procurement cycles and ROI proof; the plan contains no evidence those steps will be compressed or skipped. If pilots are required (and they usually are), the 3-month target is unlikely to be met.
flaws.question: What is the exact sales funnel and timeline that converts a cold enterprise lead into a paying annual contract within 90 days, and who has committed to each step?

flaws.title: Unknown buyer — who inside the manufacturer actually has the problem and budget?
flaws.description: The document does not specify which function (operations, maintenance, reliability engineering, procurement) is the customer decision-maker or payer. Different buyers have different success metrics, budgets, and procurement processes; failing to name and validate the buyer means the product could be built for someone who neither controls budget nor will adopt it.
flaws.question: Which exact organizational role is the target buyer, and have you validated their pain, budget authority, and procurement constraints?

flaws.title: Unstated integration/data-access assumption — product may be infeasible without OT access
flaws.description: Success assumes you can access sensor/telemetry and integrate with industrial OT systems, but this is not discussed. Manufacturers often restrict data, use legacy protocols, or require extensive on-site integration and cybersecurity approvals. If you cannot reliably access the necessary data, the monitoring AI cannot deliver the promised early-failure signals.
flaws.question: Can target customers provide the telemetry and integration access you need, and have any expressed willingness to allow that access under realistic security terms?

flaws.title: No clarity on differentiation or alternatives — who will switch from current practices?
flaws.description: The plan does not state what customers use today (manual inspections, existing analytics, OEM services) nor why they would replace those with this product. Without understanding current alternatives and the switching cost, it's unclear how you will persuade adopters to change behavior and sign an annual contract.
flaws.question: What do target customers use today to detect mechanical failure, and why will they choose your solution over that alternative?

evidence_audit.summary: Evidence base: Weak. This is a pre-launch plan with zero pilots, zero customer conversations and no validated pricing. The central revenue and early-customer claims (15 customers at $24k in 90 days) are unsupported and lack funnel or buyer-persona evidence.

flaws.title: 15 customers in 90 days is asserted but unsupported
flaws.description: The plan targets 15 enterprise customers in the first three months, which at $24,000 each implies $360,000 in annual contracts (15 × $24,000 = $360,000). There are no pilots, no sales staff, and no described pipeline or conversion rates to justify acquiring 15 large manufacturers that quickly. This is a load-bearing forecast: without concrete commitments or funnel math it is just an aspiration.
flaws.question: Provide either (A) signed commitments (contracts or LOIs) from 15 customers, or (B) a documented sales funnel showing lead volumes, staged conversion rates and timelines that mathematically produce 15 closed enterprise deals within 90 days (show the math).

flaws.title: Price point ($24k/yr) to large manufacturers is unvalidated
flaws.description: You assume each customer will pay $24,000 per year but explicitly state you have not spoken to any manufacturers and have no pilots. Willingness-to-pay at enterprise scale is load-bearing: if target buyers won't accept $24k, the revenue forecast collapses. No evidence (surveys, interviews, LOIs) is provided to support this pricing.
flaws.question: Show direct validation that the specified buyer(s) would pay $24,000/yr — e.g., documented quotes from at least five independent target buyers, signed price LOIs, or at least one paid pilot at that price.

flaws.title: Key funnel and unit economics (CAC, sales cycle, LTV) are missing
flaws.description: With a target of 15 customers, you must demonstrate acceptable acquisition cost and sales cadence. No CAC, sales-cycle length, expected conversion rates, or customer lifetime are provided, so it's impossible to judge whether the $24k ARPA supports sustainable acquisition economics. For example, if average customer lifetime is unknown, LTV cannot be computed to compare to CAC.
flaws.question: Supply your assumed or measured CAC, expected sales cycle (days), conversion rates at each funnel stage, and assumed customer lifetime (or LTV), and show the arithmetic proving those inputs support 15 customers in 90 days and acceptable payback.

flaws.title: No demand evidence — zero customer discovery or pilots
flaws.description: You state explicitly you have not spoken to any manufacturers and have no confirmed pilots. At idea/pre-launch stage this is the most direct evidence gap: without discovery interviews or a pilot, the product-market fit and practical deployability to industrial equipment operators are unknown. This prevents assessing whether the feature set and integration needs match buyer expectations.
flaws.question: Run and document at least 10 structured discovery interviews with the target buyer personas and secure at least one pilot or written pilot commitment; provide notes summarizing pain, current alternatives, and willingness to pilot/pay.

flaws.title: Target buyer and decision-maker are not specified
flaws.description: The document says 'large manufacturers' but does not specify which function pays (maintenance/operations/plant manager), company size threshold, industry vertical, or procurement process. Without a clear buyer persona you cannot design the sales approach nor judge the plausibility of rapid enterprise sign-ups.
flaws.question: Define the exact buyer persona(s) (title, department, company size and vertical) and provide evidence (interview notes or org charts) that these personas have budget authority or influence for $24k/year decisions.
